question: How did Ahmed Al Ansari build Dunes from startup to trusted Dubai business without being an Arabic speaker?
transcript_excerpt: Ahmed Al Ansari joined a legal translation company as a translation project manager, learning to manage the entire process from document intake to delivery without being a translator himself. He applied his team leadership experience from Vodafone to build a qualified team: native Arabic translators in Cairo and Alexandria, specialized project managers ensuring quality checks, and a ringmaster approach where he connects all workflow dots. His role is frontline project management and quality oversight, ensuring each line and number is correct before documents go to government departments, courts, or ministries.

question: What was Ahmed Al Ansari's first major project when he started Dunes and how much revenue did it generate?
transcript_excerpt: Ahmed Al Ansari's company started charging 35 dirham per page for translations. On the second day of operation, they received a major project from Al Maya Supermarket group involving 64,000 dirham worth of legal translation work for a court case. Al Ansari and his partner Nazir worked two days and two nights straight, sleeping in the office to deliver the project, which helped establish trust and proved their capability.

question: What is Ahmed Al Ansari's philosophy on business partnerships and why does he not discuss ownership percentages?
transcript_excerpt: Ahmed Al Ansari believes the foundation of long-term business partnership sustainability is trust, not money discussions. He never asks his partner how much money is coming into the bank account, only how many deals were closed that day. He emphasizes that if you have enough trust with your partner, there is nothing to be written on paper—mutual understanding is sufficient. His advice to entrepreneurs starting partnerships is: do not talk about money at the start, because as a Muslim, there is no Baraka (blessing) in the business if money is the first discussion.

question: Why is AI translation inadequate for legal documents according to Ahmed Al Ansari?
transcript_excerpt: Ahmed Al Ansari defines AI as a developed version of Microsoft Access and Excel that always requires human intervention. AI provides line-by-line translation but fails to deliver expressive translation that conveys emotions and narrative context—critical for legal documents. In the legal field, judges will immediately recognize AI-translated documents as inadequate. Additionally, AI cannot provide logical amendments needed when presenting legal documents. For high-value cases like a 10 million case in DIFC, clients will never accept AI translation because they hold their translation provider responsible for accuracy; a single word mistake can create disaster.

question: How does Dunes handle different Arabic dialects across GCC countries in legal translation?
transcript_excerpt: When accepting a project, Dunes uses a questionnaire to identify the end reader and their origin (Qatar, Saudi, UAE, Egypt, etc.). They also analyze the document type—whether it is technical, medical, or financial translation—and route it to a specialized translator with expertise in that domain. For example, financial documents go to translators who understand terms like FDA and Zakat. Dunes only uses native Arabic speakers as translators. This approach ensures 100% accuracy because a single word mistake can have massive impact, such as changing 1 million to 10 million in accounting documents.
